title.narrative: Rapid Response Project for Internally Displaced Persons in Rwanguba Health Zone, Rutshuru Territory

description.narrative: The displacement crisis Rutshuru territory began when clashes resumed at the end of March 2022 between the Congolese Armed Forces (FARDC) and elements of the M23 armed group, more specifically in the Jomba Groupment. The humanitarian situation deteriorated sharply in the Rutshuru and Rwanguba Health Zones when at least 10,400 households sought safety and refuge from the violent clashes in the neighbouring localities in these two health zones, mainly on the Rutshuru-Tchengerero-Jomba and Bunagana axis. As of June 14, 2022, it is reported that 11,337 households (55,803 people) have been displaced. Nearly 80%, are camping in collective centres such as schools and churches, which are now overcrowded, and the few available social amenities are extremely overwhelmed. Due to continued fighting and tensions, further movement sparks are expected. Humanitarian needs of the displaced populations continue to rise due to limited lifesaving and protection responses and unabated movements. Documented critical needs of the displaced population include food insecurity due to loss of livelihoods and livelihood assets, malnutrition due to lack of food, health risks due to lack of access to medical care, habitation in unsafe environments and exposure to harsh environmental conditions, and risks related to poor access to safe and adequate water, safe and adequate personal and household hygiene and sanitation services and facilities. Despite current ongoing humanitarian interventions, critical gaps still exist. CAFOD through its local partner SOCOAC through this project aim to provide life-saving support and support in alleviating the suffering of the most vulnerable displaced households and most vulnerable host families, specific focus being high risks persons such as people living with disabilities, the elderly, the chronically ill, female and child headed households within Rwanguba health Zone.
